newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo dinar black mkt rate firms slightly.
newsitem.headline: Yugo dinar black mkt rate firms slightly.

text.p: Yugoslavia's dinar firmed slightly to stand at 3.80-3.85 to the German mark on Thursday as cash supply on the streets ebbed, dealers said.
The dinar was changing hands at a rate of 3.9 to the mark on Wednesday.
Dealers said lack of cash allowed the dinar to firm a bit, but economists and bankers cautioned the crisis was far from over and would not exclude a possibility of a devaluation.
They called on the government to launch a set of consistent economic and monetary measures to save the dinar and restore financial discipline.

"Both the government and the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) must take over responsibility for what is happening in the economy," a banker and a member of the Yugoslav Banking Association told Reuters.
The banker insisted NBY alone could not pursue tight money policy without an equally rigorous backing by the government. He expected solution to the crisis some time by the end of February.
"The latest dinar crisis was a very predictable scenario," an economist said.

Mladjan Dinkic of the Belgrade School of Economics said the official dinar rate was not threatened as long as the central bank sticks to an unselective selling of hard currency on the local interbank forex market.
"But the wide spread between the official and the black market rate will force NBY sooner or later to limit the supply of hard currency," Dinkic said.
According to reports published by Belgrade daily Politika, around $6 million are traded on the average everyday on the local interbank forex market.
The source close to the market said NBY was buying around $500,000 a day and selling up to $5.5 million.
Some analysts linked the latest dinar plunge to political crisis, with two months of mass street protest over local election fraud shaking the ruling Socialists.
The crisis had put off few foreign investors, who decided to freeze business arrangements with Yugoslavia and wait.

"This is a very unfavourable situation. With exports falling, there is less hard currency coming to Yugoslavia. And they obviously need the money. So they had to destabilize the dinar, make people sell marks for more dinars," said an analyst who asked not to be named.
